slots.text: By means of the demonic, then, the merman would be the single individual who as the single individual was higher than the universal. The demonic has the same property as the divine: the single individual can come into an absolute relation to it. Here we have the analogy, the counterpart, of that paradox we are discussing. It therefore has a certain likeness, and the likeness can deceive. Thus the merman apparently has this proof that his silence is justified: in it he suffers all his pain. Nevertheless there is no doubt that he can speak. So he can become a tragic hero — in my view a grandiose tragic hero — if he speaks. Only a few, perhaps, would grasp where the grandeur lies. He will then have the courage to wrest from himself every self-deception about being able to make Agnete happy by his art; he will have the courage, humanly speaking, to crush Agnete. For the rest, I will make only a psychological observation here. The more selfishly Agnete has been developed, the more dazzling the self-deception will be. Indeed, it is not unthinkable that it could happen in reality that a merman, by his demonic cunning, had — humanly speaking — not only saved an Agnete but drawn something extraordinary out of her. A demon, after all, knows how to torment strength out of even the weakest human being, and in his own way he can mean very well by a person.

notes.text: Aesthetics sometimes treats something similar with its usual flirtatious trifling. The merman is saved by Agnete, and the whole affair ends with a happy marriage. A happy marriage! That is easy enough. But if ethics is to give the speech at the wedding ceremony, then, I think, it becomes another matter. Aesthetics throws the cloak of love over the merman, and then everything is forgotten. It is also careless enough to think that a marriage goes the way an auction does, where everything is sold in the condition in which it is found when the hammer falls. It only makes sure that the lovers get each other; the rest it does not care about. It ought just to see what happens afterward; but it has no time for that — it is at once in full swing clapping a new pair of lovers together. Aesthetics is the most faithless of all the sciences. Everyone who has truly loved it becomes, in a certain sense, unhappy; but whoever has never loved it is and remains a pecus — a dull beast.

slots.text: The merman stands on a dialectical knife-edge. If he is saved out of the demonic that lies in repentance, then two ways are possible. He can hold back and remain in concealment, but not rely on his cunning. In that case, as the single individual, he does not enter into an absolute relation to the demonic, but finds rest in the counter-paradox that the deity will save Agnete. (This, no doubt, is how the Middle Ages would make the movement; for by its way of thinking the merman is plainly forfeit to the monastery.) Or he can be saved by Agnete. This must not be understood as if Agnete’s love were to save him from becoming a seducer in the future (that is an aesthetic attempt at rescue, which always goes around the main point, namely the continuity of the merman’s life); for in that respect he is saved. He is saved to the extent that he becomes disclosed. He then marries Agnete. Even so, he must have recourse to the paradox. For when the single individual has come outside the universal through his guilt, he can return to it only by virtue of having come, as the single individual, into an absolute relation to the absolute. Here I will now make a remark in which I say more than has been said anywhere in what has gone before. Sin is not the first immediacy; sin is a later immediacy. In sin the single individual is already higher than the universal, in the direction of the demonic paradox, because it is a contradiction on the universal’s part to want to demand itself of someone who lacks the conditio sine qua non — the condition without which it cannot be met. If philosophy, among other things, also thought that it might occur to a human being to want to act according to its teaching, a strange comedy would come of it. An ethics that ignores sin is an altogether idle science; but if it makes sin count, then it is eo ipso — by that very fact — beyond itself. Philosophy teaches that the immediate is to be cancelled. That is true enough; but what is not true is that sin is simply the immediate, any more than faith is simply the immediate.

notes.anchorAfterEn: anywhere in what has gone before.
notes.text: In the foregoing I have deliberately kept out any consideration of the question of sin and its reality. The whole is directed at Abraham, and him I can still reach in immediate categories — that is, to the extent that I can understand him. As soon as sin comes forward, ethics goes to ruin — precisely on repentance; for repentance is the highest ethical expression, but precisely in being that, it is the deepest ethical self-contradiction.

slots.text: As soon as I move in these spheres, everything goes easily. But what has been said here does not explain Abraham either. For Abraham did not become the single individual through sin; on the contrary, he was the righteous man, God’s chosen one. So the analogy to Abraham will show itself only after the single individual has been brought to the point of being able to carry out the universal, and now the paradox repeats itself.

I can therefore understand the merman’s movements, but I cannot understand Abraham. For the merman, precisely by way of the paradox, comes to want to realize the universal. For if he remains concealed and gives himself over to all the torments of repentance, then he becomes a demon, and as such he is annihilated. If he remains concealed, but does not cleverly suppose that by being tormented himself in the bondage of repentance he can work Agnete free, then he no doubt finds peace, but he is lost to this world. If he becomes disclosed and lets himself be saved by Agnete, then he is the greatest human being I can imagine. Only aesthetics thoughtlessly supposes it is praising the power of love by having the lost one loved by an innocent girl and thereby saved; only aesthetics sees wrongly and believes that the girl is the heroine, when it is the merman who is the hero. So the merman cannot belong to Agnete unless, after having made the infinite movement of repentance, he makes one movement more: the movement by virtue of the absurd. By his own strength he can make the movement of repentance; but he also uses absolutely all his strength for it, and therefore he cannot possibly come back by his own strength and grasp actuality again. When one does not have passion enough to make either the one movement or the other, when one muddles sloppily through life, repents a little and thinks the rest will surely take care of itself, then one has renounced, once and for all, living in the idea. And then one can very easily attain the highest, and help others to it too — that is: beguile oneself and others with the notion that in the world of spirit things go as in a game of gnav, a parlor game of luck, where everything goes along any old how. One can then amuse oneself by considering how strange it is, after all, that precisely in an age when, as we know, everyone can do the highest, doubt about the immortality of the soul can be so widespread; for whoever has really made even the movement of infinity hardly doubts. The inferences passion draws are the only reliable ones — that is, the only convincing ones. Happily, existence here is more loving, more faithful, than the wise men claim; for it excludes no human being, not even the lowliest, and it fools no one — for in the world of spirit only the one who fools himself is fooled. It is everyone’s opinion, and insofar as I may venture to judge the matter it is my opinion too, that entering a monastery is not the highest. But it is by no means my opinion, for that reason, that in our age, when no one enters a monastery, everyone is greater than those deep and earnest souls who found their rest in a monastery. How many in our age have passion enough to think this, and then to judge themselves honestly? Consider merely the thought of taking time upon one’s conscience in this way: of giving conscience time, in its sleepless tirelessness, to search out every secret thought, so that, if one does not make the movement at every moment by virtue of what is noblest and holiest in a human being, one may discover with anxiety and horror — and, if by nothing else, then by anxiety lure out — the dark stirring that after all hides in every human life; whereas when one lives in company with others, one so easily forgets, so easily gets away from it, is held up in so many ways, and gets the chance to begin afresh. This thought alone, grasped with due reverence, would, I thought, chasten many a single individual in our age who already thinks he has arrived at the highest. But people care little about that in our age, which has arrived at the highest — even though no age has been so forfeit to the comic as this very one. And it is incomprehensible that it has not already happened that the age, by a generatio æquivoca — a spontaneous generation — has given birth to its own hero: the demon who will ruthlessly put on the terrible spectacle of making the whole age laugh, and making it forget that it is laughing at itself. Or what is existence worth except to be laughed at, when one has already arrived at the highest in one’s twentieth year? And yet what higher movement has the age discovered since the time when people gave up entering the monastery? Is it not a pitiful worldly wisdom, prudence, faintheartedness, that sits in the place of honor — that cravenly makes people imagine they have done the highest, and slyly keeps them from even attempting the lesser? Whoever has made the monastery movement has only one movement left: that of the absurd. How many in our age understand what the absurd is? How many in our age live so that they have renounced everything or have gotten everything? How many are merely honest enough to know what they can and cannot do? And is it not true that, insofar as one finds such people, one is most likely to find them among the less educated, and in part among women? In a kind of clairvoyance the age discloses its failing, just as someone demonic always discloses himself without understanding himself; for again and again it demands the comic. Should that really be what the age needed? Should the theater perhaps need a new play in which it was made ridiculous that someone died of love? Or would it not rather be saving for the age if such a thing happened among us, if the age were witness to such an event — so that for once it might find the courage to believe in the power of spirit, the courage to stop cravenly stifling what is better in itself and enviously stifling it in others — by laughter? Should the age really need a ridiculous Erscheinung — apparition — of someone awakened, in order to get something to laugh at? Or should it not rather need such an inspired figure to remind it of what has been forgotten?

notes.text: This is not believed in our earnest age; and yet it is remarkable enough that even in paganism — which is by its nature more frivolous and less thoroughly reflected — the two true representatives of the Greek view of existence, γνῶθι σαυτόν (know yourself), have each in his own way intimated that by going deep into oneself one discovers first and foremost the disposition to evil. That I am thinking of Pythagoras and Socrates I surely need not say.

slots.text: If one wanted a design in a similar style — one that would nevertheless be more moving, because the passion of repentance was not set in motion — one could use for it a story found in the Book of Tobit. The young Tobias wants to marry Sarah, the daughter of Raguel and Edna. There is a sad circumstance attached to this girl. She has been given to seven men, all of whom lost their lives in the bridal chamber. With regard to my design, this is a blemish on the story; for a comic effect is almost unavoidable when the thought is aroused of a girl’s seven fruitless attempts to get married, although she came very close to it — as close as a student who went up seven times for his degree examination and was failed. In the Book of Tobit the accent lies elsewhere, and therefore the high number matters there and is even, in a certain sense, a tragic contributing factor; for the young Tobias’s magnanimity is all the greater — partly insofar as he is his parents’ only son (6:15), partly because what might deter him presses itself on him all the more. So this must go. Sarah, then, is a girl who has never loved, who still keeps a young girl’s blessedness, her enormous first-priority bond on existence, her “Vollmachtbrief zum Glücke” — her letter of authority for happiness: to love a man with her whole heart. And yet she is more unhappy than anyone; for she knows the evil demon who loves her will kill the bridegroom on the wedding night. I have read about much sorrow, but I doubt that anywhere there is a sorrow as deep as the one that lies in this girl’s life. When unhappiness comes from outside, after all, there is still comfort to be found. If existence did not bring a person what could have made him happy, it is still a comfort that he could have received it. But the unfathomable sorrow that no time can dispel, no time can heal: to know that it would do no good if existence did everything! A Greek writer hides so infinitely much in his simple naivety when he says: πάντως γὰρ οὐδεὶς Ἔρωτα ἔφυγεν ἢ φεύξεται, μέχρι ἂν κάλλος ᾖ καὶ ὀφθαλμοὶ βλέπωσιν — for no one has ever escaped Eros, or ever will, as long as there is beauty and eyes can see (cf. Longus, Pastoralia). There was many a girl who became unhappy in love; but she became so — Sarah was so before she became so. It is hard not to find the one to whom one can give oneself, but it is unspeakably hard not to be able to give oneself. A young girl gives herself, and then people say: now she is no longer free. But Sarah was never free, and yet she had never given herself. It is hard if a girl gave herself and was deceived; but Sarah was deceived before she gave herself. What a world of sorrow lies in what follows, when Tobias at last means to marry her! What wedding ceremonies, what preparations! No girl has been deceived as Sarah was; for she was cheated of the most blessed thing of all, the absolute wealth that even the poorest girl possesses — cheated of the secure, boundless, unbound, unbridled self-abandon of giving herself. For first there had to be the smoking, as the heart and liver of the fish were laid on glowing embers. And how the mother must take leave of her daughter — the daughter who, just as she herself is cheated of everything, must, in continuity with this, cheat her mother of what is most beautiful! Just read the story. Edna prepared the chamber, and she led Sarah into it, and wept, and she accepted her daughter’s tears. And she said to her: Take courage, my child! May the Lord of heaven and earth give you joy for this sorrow of yours! Daughter, take courage. And now the moment of the wedding — read it, if you can for tears: But when the two of them were shut in together, Tobias rose from the bed and said: Get up, sister, and let us pray that the Lord may have mercy on us (8:4).

If a poet read this story, if he wanted to use it, I would bet a hundred to one that he would stake everything on the young Tobias. This heroism of being willing to risk his life in so evident a danger — a danger the story reminds us of once more, for Raguel, the morning after the wedding, tells Edna: Send one of the maidservants to look and see whether he is alive; but if he is not, so that I may bury him and no one shall know of it (cf. 8:13) — this heroism would become the task. I take the liberty of proposing another. It is brave, stout-hearted and chivalrous of Tobias to act as he does; but any man who does not have the courage for it is a milksop who knows neither what love is, nor what it is to be a man, nor what is worth the trouble of living for. He has not even grasped the little mystery that it is better to give than to receive, and he has no inkling of the great one: that it is far harder to receive than to give — that is, when one has had the courage to do without, and did not turn coward in the hour of distress. No, Sarah — she is the heroine. Her I want to approach as I have never approached any girl, nor felt tempted to approach in thought any girl I have read about. For what love of God it takes to be willing to let oneself be healed when one has been botched like this from the beginning, through no guilt of one’s own — from the beginning a spoiled specimen of a human being! What ethical maturity, to take upon herself the responsibility of allowing the beloved such a daring venture! What humility before another human being! What faith in God, that she would not hate, the very next moment, the man to whom she owed everything!

Let Sarah be a man, and the demonic lies close at hand. The proud, noble nature can bear everything; but one thing it cannot bear: it cannot bear pity. There lies in pity an injury that can be done to him only by a higher power; for by himself he can never become its object. If he has sinned, he can bear the punishment without despairing; but to have been singled out, without guilt, from his mother’s womb as a sacrifice to pity, a sweet savor in its nostrils — that he cannot endure. Pity has a strange dialectic: one moment it demands guilt, the next it will not have it. And so being predestined to pity becomes more and more terrible the more the individual’s misfortune lies in the direction of the spiritual. But Sarah has no guilt. She is flung aside as prey to every suffering, and on top of that she is to be tormented by people’s pity; for even I, who admire her more than Tobias loved her — even I cannot name her name without saying: the poor girl. Let a man be in Sarah’s place; let him know that if he wants to love a girl, a spirit from hell will come and murder the beloved on the wedding night. Then it might well be that he chose the demonic. He shut himself up within himself and said, in the way a demonic nature speaks in secret: “Thank you, I am no friend of ceremonies and fuss; I do not in the least demand the pleasure of love; after all, I can become a Bluebeard who takes his delight in seeing the girls sink down on the wedding night.” As a rule one gets to know very little about the demonic, even though precisely in our age this territory has a valid claim to be explored, and even though the observer, provided he knows how to put himself a little in rapport with the demon, can make use of almost any human being, at least for a moment. In this respect Shakespeare is and always remains a hero. That dreadful demon, the most demonic figure Shakespeare has portrayed — but also portrayed incomparably — Gloucester (later Richard III): what made him a demon? Obviously this: that he could not bear the pity to which he had been exposed from childhood. His monologue in Act I of Richard III is worth more than whole systems of morality that have no inkling of the horrors of existence or of their explanation.
